The BEV, rendered from scene annotations for training, depicts roads and vehicles as simple shapes at a fixed metric scale, providing a top-down view of their positions and motion with reduced occlusion between vehicles. Perspective video, by contrast, retains scene details that the BEV omits, such as traffic signals and object appearance. Joint attention between two video diffusion transformers, one per stream, lets each stream inform the other during generation. The predicted BEV also provides a geometric interface for ego control: we translate and rotate its latest frame along an input ego trajectory and use the resulting frames as a soft condition that shows how the scene would appear to move if only the ego vehicle moved. At inference, BirdDreams generates both videos from a single camera image without requiring an HD map or vehicle-state inputs. On PhysicalAI-AV and nuScenes, BirdDreams follows input ego trajectories more faithfully than prior driving world models and generates more plausible ego motion without ego-action conditioning. Human evaluation shows that BirdDreams outperforms a perspective-only baseline in generating realistic surrounding-vehicle behavior.

title: Improved last-iterate bounds for SGD with and without replacement

payload.title: Improved last-iterate bounds for SGD with and without replacement
payload.abstract: In this work, we study last-iterate convergence bounds for stochastic gradient descent (SGD) on convex and $β$-smooth loss functions and improve the bound from $\cO((\log T)^3/T)$ to $\cO((\log T)^3/(T\log\log T))$ in the interpolation regime. The improvement comes from applying a horizon-dependent multiscale estimate of gradients to the comparison of trajectories. The bound applies to both sampling with replacement and sampling without replacement within one pass.

title: OverServe: Resource Amplification Attacks on SaaS Agents via Tool--Prompt Co-Design

payload.title: OverServe: Resource Amplification Attacks on SaaS Agents via Tool--Prompt Co-Design
payload.abstract: Advances in large language models (LLMs) are enabling software-as-a-service (SaaS) providers to automate longer business workflows with agents. In subscription-based SaaS deployments, model and tool calls consume provider resources without additional customer payments. Because the agent autonomously decides when to stop, a malicious tenant can send a prompt to the agent, exploiting its completion decisions to extend execution and waste provider resources. In this paper, we present OverServe, a multi-agent framework for constructing such attacks against SaaS agents. OverServe co-designs Model Context Protocol (MCP) status tools and completion-confirmation prompts for the attacker. Each tool call returns accurate status and terminates normally, yet the agent may repeatedly check an unfinished condition to satisfy the prompt. This consumes the SaaS provider's resources even after the original business task is completed. OverServe constructs service-specific tool--prompt pairs and uses separate tool and prompt reviews to guide candidate pair selection. Tested tool specifications trigger no alerts in the evaluated MCP scanners. We evaluate Qwen, Nemotron, DeepSeek, and Sonnet on selected tasks from nine benchmarks. All OverServe runs pass the original task checks. OverServe can reach a maximal amplification of API requests by $93.88\times$ while preserving the original task goal and collateral checks.

title: GenPFN: An In-Context Tabular Foundation Model Approach for Augmenting Small Datasets in Engineering

payload.title: GenPFN: An In-Context Tabular Foundation Model Approach for Augmenting Small Datasets in Engineering
payload.abstract: Costly simulations and experiments limit the data available for engineering design. This paper proposes GenPFN, a training-free candidate generator guided by a pretrained tabular Prior-Data Fitted Network (TabPFN) classifier with fixed weights. The context contains evaluated designs labeled desired (Class 1) or undesired (Class 0). GenPFN interpolates between desired designs and refines candidates using gated classifier gradients and Gaussian noise. Each candidate is evaluated using the problem's constraints and objective functions. Evaluated desired designs and their objective values augment the context for regression training. Evaluation spans fourteen selected problems, including a two-parameter benchmark and a 44-parameter hull problem. In paired comparisons, GenPFN with TabPFN v1 achieves higher class satisfaction and lower realism distance than the tested adversarial, variational-autoencoder and diffusion generators. The variational-autoencoder generator provides greater coverage and diversity. Relative to the synthetic minority over-sampling technique (SMOTE), GenPFN provides lower coverage distance and greater diversity. Among observed paired regression fits, augmentation reduces estimated AutoGluon validation mean squared error by 62.1% relative to context-only training. A hull-stern case study yields 99.3% propeller-compatible candidates versus 1.4% among randomly sampled context designs. Generation followed by evaluation produces sample sets that augment limited datasets and support training more accurate predictive models.

title: When Is Proof-Step Verification Worth Its Cost? Operating Requirements of Certify-or-Decline Verification for Open-Weight Mathematical Reasoning

payload.title: When Is Proof-Step Verification Worth Its Cost? Operating Requirements of Certify-or-Decline Verification for Open-Weight Mathematical Reasoning
payload.abstract: Proof-step verification rewrites a solver's answer into typed steps and uses LLM judges to certify or decline. We evaluate this pipeline on open-weight models across GPQA, AIME-2025, and a MATH-500 subset. Certification raises answer-key-match precision by 31 percentage points on the strong GPQA configuration and 46 on AIME, while answering only 35% and 21% of attempts. On near-ceiling MATH-500, gains are at most 5 points at a loss of 13-27 points of coverage. An output-token-matched self-consistency selector obtains 82.9% precision at 35% coverage, compared with the verifier's pooled 87.6% (paired difference: +4.8 points, 95% interval [-8.2, 18.5]). A diagnostic sample reveals a distinct failure mode: 52 of 88 completed problems end in invalid proof construction without ever reaching a judge. Finally, external-LLM acceptance of rendered certified chains is 61.0-67.6%, compared with 87.6% answer-key match. These audits lack human or formal-kernel ground truth. Open-weight auditor pairs show near-zero chance-corrected agreement, which measures consistency rather than accuracy against proof truth. These results motivate separate reporting of execution failures, selected-answer precision, and independently assessed proof validity. We provide per-configuration results and evaluation details in the supplement.

title: Mach2: Scientific Discovery Platform with Deterministic Execution Constraints

payload.title: Mach2: Scientific Discovery Platform with Deterministic Execution Constraints
payload.abstract: Language-model agents can formulate workflows and invoke specialized tools, yet compliance with natural-language operating rules is not guaranteed by prompting alone. Mach2 addresses this limitation by coupling Eigen orchestration to deterministic, lint-like checks of tool requests, source changes, acceptance tests, and artifact contracts. Domain requirements are represented as executable predicates: mandatory failures prevent advancement of the checked operation, while diagnostic findings are retained for correction or review. User-specified test-driven development (TDD), CodeGrapher's abstract-syntax-tree analysis, and history-guided evolutionary search provide complementary verification and optimization mechanisms. Mach2 also generates task-specific agent packages for execution through independently selected endpoints. The originating harness validates returned artifacts against declared interfaces and evidence requirements without assuming continuous supervision of the remote run. Model-internal-knowledge (MIK) dependencies are recorded separately from source-grounded and test-supported findings. This paper formalizes the rule-gated execution model and the agent-package lifecycle, and proposes measurable criteria for evaluating rule compliance, engineering validity, and cross-endpoint task continuity.

title: SlipStream: Enabling HBF for GPU Systems by Mitigating the Latency and SRAM Overheads

payload.title: SlipStream: Enabling HBF for GPU Systems by Mitigating the Latency and SRAM Overheads
payload.abstract: Large language model (LLM) inference demands ever more memory capacity for larger models and batch sizes. High-Bandwidth Flash (HBF) replaces the DRAM dies of HBM with NAND flash and provides up to 16x the capacity at comparable read bandwidth. However, HBF can incur a read latency of nearly 20$μ$s, 20x that of HBM, so on-demand HBF accesses slow inference by up to 12.8x. Conventional cache-line prefetchers require 20x more in-flight tracking state to cover this latency. Tensor-streaming designs, such as H3, follow virtual-address order as opposed to kernel-demand order, and therefore need hundreds of megabytes of buffering. We propose SlipStream, a software-hardware co-designed prefetcher that turns prefetching into a demand-paced producer-consumer pipeline. In software, SlipStream profiles the repeatable weight-page demand order of data-independent LLM kernels and inserts a staging warp that replays this order with non-blocking STAGE instructions. In hardware, the staging warp acts as the producer and the work warps as consumers. Our key insight is to retire each STAGE tracking entry only when demand first accesses the page, as opposed to when the page returns from HBF. Demand thus paces staging and bounds how far staging leads consumption. SlipStream tracks 4 KB pages instead of cache lines and allocates buffer slots only when pages return, which decouples the buffer size from outstanding traffic. Across seven dense models spanning 16-800 GB, SlipStream with a 40 MB staging buffer achieves 92.4% of the performance of an ideal HBF with HBM-like latency. H3 achieves only 43.1%, even with a 320 MB buffer. The buffer sizing of SlipStream is independent of HBF latency and workload. SlipStream with 16 MB buffer, 20x smaller than that of H3, performs within 4% of SlipStream-40MB. SlipStream also supports Mixture-of-Experts models and reaches 91.2% of ideal performance (40 MB buffer).

title: Leaderboard Hacking: Preference-Based Model Evaluations are Vulnerable to Manipulation

payload.title: Leaderboard Hacking: Preference-Based Model Evaluations are Vulnerable to Manipulation
payload.abstract: Arena-style rankings of language models are a widely used evaluation framework in online leaderboards, research papers, and model evaluation in production. These rankings aim to realistically assess model performance using pairwise comparisons of anonymous models on user prompts, aggregating votes via the Bradley-Terry model to produce the final ranking. However, we find that these leaderboards are highly vulnerable to several manipulation strategies that unscrupulous providers could use to boost a model's rank: strategic voting (individual votes that boost a model's rank, including votes on irrelevant models), strategic prompting (choosing prompts that favor a model), and strategic nomination (boosting the rank of a model by inserting irrelevant models). We demonstrate these effects on public leaderboard data, analyze the circumstances that cause these vulnerabilities, and describe approaches to safeguard against each attack. Notably, these issues hold for any preference-based evaluation using the Bradley-Terry model that allows open prompting, voting, or model submission. These manipulations boost the rank of nearly every tested model; each attack can boost a model by up to 15-20 places in a ranking and, combined, they can boost a model by up to 45 places.

title: Rational Use of Time for Social Coordination in Humans and AI

payload.title: Rational Use of Time for Social Coordination in Humans and AI
payload.abstract: All social interactions are situated in time. Previous studies have shown that humans are able to use implicit temporal cues, such as the duration of a pause, to infer others' mental states. But how do humans use temporal cues for dynamic, fine-grained social coordination? And can AI systems do the same, without ``experiencing'' continuous real-time as humans do? We study these questions using a cooperative card game task called The Mind, which requires players to achieve a shared goal across repeated interactions but forbids explicit communication: the only available signal is the passage of time. We evaluate 150 humans, and two classes of AI models which reflect different ways of operationalizing time in artificial systems: computer-use agents (CUAs), and standard text-prompted LLMs. We find that human behavior is best captured by a Bayesian strategy that infers a partner's belief from their timing---and similarly for frontier models. However, unlike humans, none of the tested models seem to efficiently adapt their behaviors to their partners' over the course of the game. From a cognitive perspective, our findings suggest that humans perform implicit probabilistic reasoning about continuous-time signals in dynamic social settings, and that such reasoning mechanisms may emerge without real-time experience. Practically, our study highlights new challenges for AI systems to coordinate efficiently with other agents by learning to interpret and adapt to their implicit signals in dynamic settings.

title: SynthCorp: A Platform for Creating Benchmarks for Data Agents

payload.title: SynthCorp: A Platform for Creating Benchmarks for Data Agents
payload.abstract: Current benchmarks for LLM-driven data agents saturate quickly and cannot target specific capabilities. We present SynthCorp, a platform that creates customizable data estates and benchmarks by simulating how business events produce and modify corporate data over time. Each data estate combines relational databases, a document store, and a data catalog, paired with evaluation tasks and executable gold programs. First, given a scenario and target complexity dimensions, SynthCorp synthesizes reusable event types and compiles each into a program over predefined simulation primitives. Second, SynthCorp schedules event instances on a virtual calendar, interleaving routine and disruption events so that tables, documents, and catalog entries remain consistent. Third, SynthCorp executes the calendar to materialize the data estate and records every operation in a simulation log. Fourth, SynthCorp generates analytical tasks and derives verified gold programs from the log. We use SynthCorp to generate initial evaluation benchmarks comprising seven data estates (up to 1K operational tables) and 256 tasks across five domains. The data estates pass deterministic pipeline checks (such as foreign-key violations, undeclared writes, recurrence violations, and database execution failures) with a near-zero error rate, introduce cross-asset complexities, and cover all requested dimensions. Evaluating three models across four data-context settings shows that the benchmarks separate data contexts and model tiers. Auditing candidate queries against causal provenance in the simulation log verifies gold programs without manual annotation, including on multi-event composite tasks that expose reasoning failures in state-of-the-art agents. We hope the community uses SynthCorp to generate more challenging and useful data estates and benchmarks that foster the development of enterprise data agents.

title: RECALL: Real-Time Recalibration of Multi-Camera Rigs via Learned OEM-Anchored Residuals

payload.title: RECALL: Real-Time Recalibration of Multi-Camera Rigs via Learned OEM-Anchored Residuals
payload.abstract: Multi-camera rigs ship pre-calibrated from the manufacturer, but their calibration goes stale each time the rig is repositioned, and drifts continuously through wear, thermal cycling, and vibration. Recovering it on-the-fly is hard: classical bundle adjustment needs a fresh multi-view capture and a global optimization whose cost grows with the rig, ruling out real-time use. In this paper we present RECALL, a feed-forward method that recalibrates a movable multi-camera rig in a single pass. From the nominal OEM calibration as an anchor and a brief observation of a known object, it predicts each camera's current intrinsics and extrinsics, written as a shared global rotation of the rig composed with a small per-camera drift. Instead of regressing the calibration in one shot, RECALL refines its estimate with a learned, rig-coupled recurrent operator that reprojects through a differentiable projection and applies attention across the cameras at each step, and solves for the shared rotational gauge in-network with a learned Gauss-Newton step rather than regressing it. Because the ground truth is synthesizable, we train entirely on data generated on-the-fly and need no captured dataset. On a synthetic 10-camera benchmark, RECALL is more accurate than per-camera and rig-coupled joint bundle adjustment ($0.26^\circ$ vs $0.47^\circ$ rotation, $5.4$ vs $8.9$ px focal) and runs about $10^5\times$ faster at about $0.12$ ms per rig. On real data (TotalCapture, CMU Panoptic) it matches or beats offline rig-coupled bundle adjustment on absolute and relative rotation while running four-to-five orders of magnitude faster, and on the Panoptic surround rig it also matches the strongest image-only foundation models (VGGT, VGGT-$Ω$, $π^3$) on relative pose while staying metric and about $15\times$ more accurate in focal length. Code: https://github.com/theICTlab/RECALL-multicam

title: Benchmarking Multilingual Document Understanding in Vision-Language Models

payload.title: Benchmarking Multilingual Document Understanding in Vision-Language Models
payload.abstract: Recent Vision-Language Models (VLMs) perform strongly on multimodal tasks, Document Understanding (DU) among them, but the benchmarks that measure them mostly cover English documents and narrow problems. How well current VLMs generalize across languages, tasks, styles and layouts therefore remains unclear. We introduce MDU, a multilingual DU benchmark of 23146 examples spanning 13 tasks and five languages: English, French, German, Italian, and Spanish. The tasks isolate complementary capabilities, from surface-level text and Markdown extraction through summarization, classification and named-entity recognition to layout-sensitive passage and layout extraction. We evaluate 45 state-of-the-art open-weight VLMs from 1.7B to 235B parameters, plus one commercial system under the same protocol. The benchmark is far from saturated: the best average is 69.0, only eight of the 45 evaluated systems reach 65, and the two best results come from 27B models rather than from the largest systems we evaluate. Performance is uneven in ways that scale does not fix. The gap between the strongest and weakest language does not close as models grow, and it survives controlling for the domain composition of each language. Capabilities also do not improve together: once we partial out overall model quality, per-task scores are largely uncorrelated, and transcription ability in particular trades off against semantic extraction.

title: A New Framework for Quantum Reinforcement Learning

payload.title: A New Framework for Quantum Reinforcement Learning
payload.abstract: Quantum reinforcement learning (QRL) has emerged as a promising approach for controlling quantum systems and accelerating learning tasks with quantum resources. However, most existing QRL formulations still retain a classical reinforcement learning interface: states and actions are often encoded in computational bases and rewards are extracted through measurements. This interface is restrictive for genuinely quantum environments: choosing a measurement can discard entanglement information, while repeated intermediate measurements collapse the evolving state and require costly re-preparation. This motivates a fully QRL framework in which the agent, environment, rewards, and return accumulation are all quantum. In this paper, we take a step toward this goal and introduce a new QRL framework in which both the policy and the environment are modeled by conditional quantum channels. We then propose a quantum policy-gradient algorithm for parameterized conditional quantum channels with a trainable control basis. We also derive finite- and infinite-horizon gradient estimators using a new parameter-shift rule. This rule is needed because policy parameters are shared across repeated interaction blocks and the infinite-horizon objective is not a finite circuit; rather than shifting every occurrence and evaluating the whole trajectory, our estimator shifts only one sampled policy block. Sampling this block from a geometric distribution yields an unbiased gradient estimator under bounded rewards. Finally, we establish convergence of the resulting stochastic gradient-ascent procedure to stationary points under standard smoothness and step-size assumptions.

title: SyntheIce: A Synthetic Radargram Annotation Benchmark for Englacial Layer Reconstruction

payload.title: SyntheIce: A Synthetic Radargram Annotation Benchmark for Englacial Layer Reconstruction
payload.abstract: Englacial layers in radio-echo-sounding radargrams (subsurface ice images) encode the climate and flow history of ice sheets and glaciers. However, large-scale extraction is hindered by time-consuming manual annotation and semi-automated detectors that produce fragmented rather than continuous horizons. We address two challenges: reconstructing complete layers from partial detections across radargram profiles and validating layer continuity across adjacent tile boundaries. We introduce a slope-aware greedy fragment-linking algorithm that reconstructs full-width layers using row-similarity gating and an exponentially weighted moving average (EWMA) slope predictor. Each reconstruction receives a content-based hash ID for stable cross-radargram identification. For quantitative evaluation, we generate SyntheIce, a synthetic dataset of 600 radargrams spanning multiple complexity levels and realistic noise conditions, including 150 wide radargrams divided into four adjacent tiles. All samples include exact ground-truth annotations. We evaluate the dataset using XCheck, a consistency-based validation framework, extending its original two-image setting to four consecutive tiles and enforcing continuity at every boundary. This demonstrates the dataset's utility for developing and evaluating real-world annotation algorithms. Our findings extend beyond ice science: when spatial features are fragmented but retain consistent local geometry, trajectory-based linking is more reliable than appearance-based matching. Evaluation against expert-labeled real radargrams demonstrates high precision, recall, F1-score, and mean IoU, supporting the method's transfer to real-world data.

title: Robbing Peter to Pay Paul: Cross-Attribute Externalities of Fairness Interventions

payload.title: Robbing Peter to Pay Paul: Cross-Attribute Externalities of Fairness Interventions
payload.abstract: Fairness interventions often targets disparities associated with a single sensitive attribute in binary classification tasks. However, when multiple sensitive attributes are associated with a data subject, improving fairness with respect to one attribute does not necessarily improve it across all attributes: it may exacerbate disparities associated with other sensitive attributes, including those that are unavailable to the practitioner. We refer to these unintended effects as cross-attribute externalities of fairness. We study how fairness with respect to one sensitive attribute varies when an initially unfair classification or regression model is corrected with respect to another attribute. We characterize these externalities using Wasserstein barycentric disparities and develop a distributional framework that captures changes in both marginal and joint fairness measures. This highlights a limitation of conventional fairness evaluation, in which the success of an intervention is assessed mainly for the attribute it targets. In a jointly Gaussian model, we derive explicit trajectories for marginal and joint disparities and identify conditions under which an intervention eliminates disparities with respect to its target attribute while increasing disparities associated with another attribute. We also derive sharp partial-identification bounds on the resulting externalities when a sensitive attribute is unavailable and extend our results to categorical sensitive attributes. We illustrate these externalities using classification and regression real-data: in the classification experiments, interventions increase unfairness with respect to the hidden attribute in the majority of scenarios across more than half of the datasets considered; in the regression experiments on the ACSIncome dataset, correcting for race reduces sex disparities, whereas subsequently correcting for age increases them.

title: The Rebundling of Freelance Work in the AI Age

payload.title: The Rebundling of Freelance Work in the AI Age
payload.abstract: This paper examines how freelance work is changing in the AI era. We compare the activities people undertake in ChatGPT with the work clients request on Upwork, an online freelance platform, and examine how clients combine tasks into projects. We find that activities more prevalent in ChatGPT tend to lose marketplace share on Upwork, while those less prevalent tend to gain share. Within AI-related work, demand is becoming more diverse, and job postings combine tasks that were rarely requested together before the generative AI era. AI-related postings also have substantially larger project budgets and involve more hours of work, while differences in hourly rates are small. Together, these findings suggest that AI is reshaping not only which tasks clients outsource, but also how they combine tasks into larger, higher-value projects.

title: Beyond Foreign-Key Connectivity: Semantic Relationship Representation for Relational Deep Learning

payload.title: Beyond Foreign-Key Connectivity: Semantic Relationship Representation for Relational Deep Learning
payload.abstract: Relational databases encode information through tables and primary--foreign key constraints. Although recent Relational Deep Learning (RDL) approaches represent these databases as heterogeneous graphs, a foreign-key connection primarily specifies structural connectivity between records. Its semantic interpretation may involve additional information that is not explicitly represented by connectivity alone. This paper introduces a conceptual framework for constructing relationship-aware representations from relational databases. The framework distinguishes three complementary aspects: (i) schema-defined relationship semantics, including endpoint types and foreign-key roles; (ii) association entities and explicitly available relationship-level attributes; and (iii) contextual information describing the temporal and structural circumstances of a connection. We formulate a Relationship Representation Construction (RRC) protocol that maps relational schema elements and database records to node representations, relationship descriptors, and contextual representations. A key principle of the protocol is semantic ownership: attributes are assigned to records, relationships, or context according to their meaning, rather than merely their physical location in a database table. Ambiguous attributes are not automatically promoted to relationship features. The resulting representations can be incorporated into existing relational graph learning architectures through relationship-conditioned message passing. The proposed framework is complementary to recent work on relational message passing, graph transformers, and task-dependent graph construction. We discuss its conceptual foundations, illustrate the construction protocol using a multi-table database, and identify research questions and empirical evaluations required to establish its potential benefits.

title: Conformal Risk Certificates for Portfolio Optimization Under Uncertainty: A Gated Reinforcement-Learning Approach

payload.title: Conformal Risk Certificates for Portfolio Optimization Under Uncertainty: A Gated Reinforcement-Learning Approach
payload.abstract: Reinforcement-learning portfolio policies can optimize allocations from prices, covariances, and prior positions, yet they lack a calibrated, replayable mechanism for certifying that a proposed allocation respects a bounded risk envelope before execution. Regulators increasingly expect automated portfolio systems to provide exactly this kind of pre-trade audit trail, interpretable risk limit, and human-oversight mechanism. Gated Conformal Semantic Risk Control addresses this gap by separating return-seeking allocation from text-conditioned downside-risk verification. An instruction-tuned language model maps timestamped disclosures into schema-validated semantic risk states over macro, liquidity, earnings, and sector channels. These states induce correlated ellipsoidal factor-shock uncertainty sets whose conformal radii are calibrated by rolling finite-sample prediction over localized semantic nonconformity buckets. An asymmetric second-order cone gate then checks each raw PPO proposal against a certified worst-case semantic loss budget. The gate stays inactive for compliant proposals and intervenes only when that budget is exceeded. In walk-forward out-of-sample tests on nine liquid U.S. Select Sector SPDR ETFs, Raw PPO earns a 12.7% annual return while incurring a 4.05% semantic violation rate. Gated-CSRC removes all observed out-of-sample semantic limit breaches while retaining an 11.7% annual return. This 100-basis-point auditable safety premium is smaller than the yield loss imposed by unconditional hard projection, and exact McNemar testing confirms the compliance gain at $p < 10^{-15}$. Loughran-McDonald lexicon controls and time-shuffled text controls fail to reproduce this certificate.

title: Beyond Row-Level Prediction: Evaluating and Learning Composition for Reusable Table Representations

payload.title: Beyond Row-Level Prediction: Evaluating and Learning Composition for Reusable Table Representations
payload.abstract: Tables are compositional, with content spread across a schema, cell values, rows, and columns. Large-scale operations such as retrieval, overlap estimation, deduplication, and data curation need these local signals composed into one reusable embedding vector per table. Table representation methods, however, are mostly evaluated through row-level prediction or supervised downstream tasks, which do not measure table-level embedding quality directly. We introduce a benchmark that evaluates table-level embeddings through four desiderata: consistency under partial views, discriminability across label granularities, robustness to benign perturbations, and efficiency. Across twelve methods on synthetic and real corpora, lightweight schema- and text-based fingerprints are among the strongest. The sharpest contrast comes from two tabular foundation models, TabPFN and ConTextTab: although both are strong row-level predictors, their states, composed by mean, max, or three further parameter-free pooling rules, trail the strongest fingerprints. We therefore ask whether the gap lies in the encoder or in the compositional rule. Keeping ConTextTab frozen, we learn only the compositional rule over its cell states, using support-conditioned distribution matching (SCDM), a self-supervised loss we propose that matches the distribution of embedding similarities to the distribution of partition overlaps within and across tables. Across all fifteen head configurations, the learned rule raises the Spearman correlation between embedding similarity and partial-view overlap from 0.04 to 0.43-0.50 on synthetic data and improves triplet ranking, clustering, and retrieval, with smaller but systematic gains on real data. A downstream parent-table retrieval task confirms these findings. How local states are composed, and with what objective, substantially affects the quality of table-level embeddings.

title: Risk-Aware Joint Inference and Resource Control for Physical AI in 6G Networks

payload.title: Risk-Aware Joint Inference and Resource Control for Physical AI in 6G Networks
payload.abstract: Wireless edge inference enables Physical-AI devices to execute edge-inferred actions using transmitted sensory inputs. Since the risk of incorrect actions vary across observations and tasks, the associated uplink transmission of sensory inputs requires different levels of wireless reliability. For instance, applying a fixed signal-to-interference-plus-noise ratio (SINR) requirement can overprovision low-risk tasks while underprovisioning high-risk ones. Therefore, we propose risk-aware control for edge inference (RACE), which maps predicted action-failure probability and task criticality to adaptive SINR targets and combines them with deadline-derived SINR requirements. A slow-timescale large language model (LLM) proposes task requirements for deterministic validation, while a fast hybrid actor selects inference configurations and transmit power levels, complemented by analytical receive beamforming and finite power restoration. Simulations show $11\%$ improvement in the average accuracy-latency-energy objective over fixed-high-SINR control, with near-zero constraint outage.

title: Trait Hitchhiking in LLM Post-Training

payload.title: Trait Hitchhiking in LLM Post-Training
payload.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) is now a standard stage of language model post-training, and the compute devoted to it is growing rapidly. While it has been shown to improve capabilities, particularly for tasks with verifiable rewards, it can also change behaviours and internal properties that the reward does not explicitly target. We present a formalism to describe the evolution of "traits" during RL post-training and, in doing so, recover the Price equation from evolutionary biology. We use this to develop a mathematical model for what we call "trait hitchhiking": the amplification or suppression of non-targeted traits as training redistributes probability across completions. We evaluate this Price update expression on language models trained with GRPO and show that the Price estimates closely track the sampled trait dynamics. These results identify trait hitchhiking as a mechanism by which RL post-training can silently amplify undesirable traits.

title: Together Compiler: Continual Compilation for AI Inference

payload.title: Together Compiler: Continual Compilation for AI Inference
payload.abstract: Today's AI workloads are rapidly changing: new models are released more often, model architectures are increasingly diverse, and traffic distributions change frequently. The challenge we face at Together AI is continual optimization for these changing workloads. Compiling a deployment into an optimized forward pass is a challenge that is well-suited for agent hill-climbing. Existing systems struggle with continual compilation due to a tradeoff between measurement throughput and fidelity. Many systems use agents to optimize individual kernels from the inference forward pass using offline benchmarks, but timings are low-fidelity because of data-dependent behavior in primitives like mixture-of-experts (MoE). On the other hand, systems use agents to directly optimize end-to-end engines but suffer from slow engine launch times. To address these challenges, we build Together Compiler (TKCC), the first truly continual agent loop designed for AI inference optimization. To address the throughput-fidelity tradeoff, we propose: (1) a Tiered Persistent Engine that decouples engine launch overheads from forward pass computation; (2) a cost model to select the parallelism configurations that seed the optimization process. We also conduct extensive ablations on agent context management and present our insights on deploying TKCC in production. TKCC outperforms highly-optimized hand-written Megakernels on the Llama 1B workhorse workload by up to 1.7x and the best open source engines on the latest frontier models (Kimi K3, GLM 5.3, MiniMax M3.1 Flash, DeepSeek v4.1 Flash) across hardware platforms by up to 2.6x higher TPS on the InferenceX benchmark. TKCC also sets the state-of-the-art performance at batch size 1, with 1111 TPS on M3.1 Flash and 1205 TPS on DeepSeek v4.1 Flash. Finally, TKCC generalizes beyond frontier language model inference. TKCC serves trillions of tokens across our production fleet.

title: MITRA-Swarm: Injecting Explicit Linguistic Structure into Foundation Models for Classical Machine Translation

payload.title: MITRA-Swarm: Injecting Explicit Linguistic Structure into Foundation Models for Classical Machine Translation
payload.abstract: Classical Sanskrit poses three challenges unresolved by single-call monolithic models: morphophonemic fusion Sandhi, dense nominal compounding Samāsa, and discourse-level zero-anaphora forced by poetic meter. We present MITRA-Swarm, a multi-agent architecture injecting explicit linguistic structure into an otherwise monolithic pipeline: a Sandhi-splitting agent, a parallel array of generalist gemma-4-26B-A4B-it and domain-specialized gemma-2-mitra-it translators, and a discourse-aware Ellipsis Restorer that consults corpus-derived register tags to avoid inventing active-voice subjects in impersonal legal and philosophical registers. Two separated judges evaluate quality: a routing judge ($J_{\text{route}}$, same model family as the generators) driving an internal critique loop, and an independent reporting judge ($J_{\text{report}}=$gpt-4o-mini, no shared vendor lineage) scoring every output exactly once. On a stratified benchmark of 1,000 verses across five registers (23,990 scored verdicts, 12-condition pre-registered ablation), the full swarm reaches $85.90$ MQM against a monolithic baseline of $85.27$ ($Δ=+0.63$, $p_{\text{adj}}=0.0018$, 95% CI $[+0.30,+0.97]$), and isolated discourse restoration alone accounts for $+0.44$ MQM ($p_{\text{adj}}=0.0288$), outperforming a call-count-matched self-refinement baseline by $+0.51$ MQM ($p_{\text{adj}}=0.0288$). Severe per-verse failures (MQM$<80$) fall from $9.0\%$ to $7.6\%$, at roughly $9\times$ the per-verse inference cost of the baseline. Additionally, $J_{\text{route}}$ scores its own family's outputs $2$-$7$ MQM higher than $J_{\text{report}}$ on every one of the 12 conditions, empirically motivating the two-judge split; and a preflight screen of a 192,151-entry retrieval index against all 12 evaluation works verifies 0 reference leaks across 269 runtime checks. These are small gains on a metric saturating near 85-86.

title: Outcome Over Learning? Evidence from Student Use of AI Code Assistants for Unit Test Writing

payload.title: Outcome Over Learning? Evidence from Student Use of AI Code Assistants for Unit Test Writing
payload.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) code assistants are rapidly being adopted in programming education, yet little is known about how students naturally use these tools when given unrestricted access. In a user study investigating AI-assisted unit test writing, we observed that a majority of students adopted a one-shot interaction strategy, asking the AI to generate a complete unit test directly from the initial requirements. While this approach is capable of efficiently producing a solution, it shifts students' focus from learning how to write effective unit tests to simply completing the task. Moreover, because students rarely engaged in critically evaluating, refining, or iterating on AI-generated output, they may be missing opportunities to develop the critical thinking skills that are essential for effective and responsible use of AI. In an effort to shift student focus from outcome to learning we also discuss how training, accountability and improved learning task design can better support a more learning-centric responsible use of AI.

title: Cleaning an Agent's History Hurts When the World Still Holds the Error

payload.title: Cleaning an Agent's History Hurts When the World Still Holds the Error
payload.abstract: Tool-using language-model agents accumulate histories of their own mistakes, and a system that compacts, repairs or hands off such a history decides what it says about those mistakes while their effects stay in the world. Prior work cleans the history at a fixed world, where showing a corrected step and saying it is done move together. We ask whether the same correct content helps or hurts depending on how the history states it and what the world holds. We freeze an agent mid-task with its exact world state, edit the history or the world, and let a receiver model continue. On AgentCE-Bench, after the agent commits a wrong value, we hold the world fixed and add the correct value by two natural edits: a truthful note beside the preserved error or the agent's own completed action. The note raises recovery, the share of remaining targets the receiver gets right, from 51% under a matched neutral note to 66%. The completed action lowers it below the unedited history, from 50% to 44%, so the value's presence alone does not predict the effect. On AppWorld, after a database write, we vary whether its receipt reports success or failure and whether its effect is present. A success receipt lowers whole-task success from 45% to 28% while the effect is absent and raises it from 38% to 49% once present. The two effects differ by 27 points pooled over two receivers, a difference positive in six of eight receivers at 97.5% and seven at 95%. A history edit's effect thus depends on the world it describes, and a history made to look clean while the world still holds the error can leave an agent worse off than no edit at all.

title: Multiple-Choice Secretary Problem with Predictions

payload.title: Multiple-Choice Secretary Problem with Predictions
payload.abstract: We study the multiple-choice secretary problem, in which candidates arrive in uniformly random order and the goal is to select at most $k$ candidates to maximize their total value. We consider a setting where predictions of individual candidate values are available before any candidate arrives. Fujii and Yoshida's Learned Kleinberg algorithm achieves competitive loss $O(\min\{\log k/\sqrt{k},\eps\})$, where $k$ is the selection capacity and $\eps$ is the maximum multiplicative prediction error. We remove the logarithmic factor through a sharper analysis of the same switching algorithm with a retuned threshold. The resulting competitive ratio is at least $\max\{0,1-\min\{32/\sqrt{k},4\eps\}\}$. In particular, exact predictions ($\eps=0$) achieve the offline optimum on every arrival order.

title: Evaluating AI Musical Creativity: Towards a Quantitative Multi-Dimensional Framework Based on Value, Novelty, and Surprise

payload.title: Evaluating AI Musical Creativity: Towards a Quantitative Multi-Dimensional Framework Based on Value, Novelty, and Surprise
payload.abstract: Despite the increasing sophistication of generative Artificial Intelligence (AI), research on the evaluation of AI-generated musical creativity remains limited. To address this gap, this paper proposes a quantitative framework for the formalization and evaluation of AI musical creativity. Building on Margaret Boden's theory, which conceptualizes creativity in terms of value, novelty, and surprise, the framework adapts and operationalizes these three dimensions for the musical domain. On the hypothesis that certain aspects of musical creativity can be assessed with a degree of objectivity, a domain-specific set of quantitative metrics for evaluating the creativity of AI-generated music is introduced. Rather than reducing musical creativity to a single unifying measure, this article proposes an ensemble of complementary metrics that capture its different dimensions, recognizing the complexity of musical artifacts and the difficulty of defining meaningful multi-objective compositional criteria. The framework has two implications. First, it gives researchers and developers a principled methodology and quantitative tools for empirically evaluating creative outputs, enabling more informed model development and reducing unnecessary computational costs. Second, it lays the groundwork for future generative models to optimize directly for creativity by adopting these metrics as learning objectives.

title: FreeDeshadow: Shadow Removal for User-Specified Objects With Multimodal Prompts

payload.title: FreeDeshadow: Shadow Removal for User-Specified Objects With Multimodal Prompts
payload.abstract: Existing shadow removal methods either perform global shadow removal or rely on precise shadow masks to guide restoration. Such paradigms limit their ability to selectively remove the shadow cast by a user-specified object in practical applications. To this end, we introduce an object-aware controllable shadow removal task, which allows users to specify a target object through a simple prompt and removes only its cast shadow while preserving other content. However, object-shadow asymmetry makes it challenging to establish accurate correspondence between the specified object and its spatially separated cast shadow and to confine restoration to the target shadow region. To address these challenges, we propose FreeDeshadow, a unified controllable shadow removal framework that supports both visual and textual prompts. It consists of an object-aware generator and a shadow-aware local refiner. The former interprets the user prompt and produces a high-quality shadow-free proposal, while the latter establishes the correspondence between the object and its cast shadow and constrains the generated changes to the target shadow region. To support training and evaluation, we further construct PCSRD+, a large-scale dataset containing 154,571 quadruples at 1024$\times$1024 resolution and covering six types of user prompts. The visual prompts include a dot, a line, and an object mask, while the textual prompts describe the target object using attributes, spatial relations, or states. Extensive experiments demonstrate that FreeDeshadow accurately removes the shadow of the target object under both visual and textual prompts while effectively preserving non-target regions. It also outperforms existing methods in shadow removal performance and controllability. Project Page: https://wzlwlm13.github.io/FreeDeshadow

title: KernelMosaic: An Open Dataset and Agentic Framework for CUDA Kernel Generation

payload.title: KernelMosaic: An Open Dataset and Agentic Framework for CUDA Kernel Generation
payload.abstract: Training large language models to generate efficient CUDA kernels requires supervision spanning diverse computational requirements and iterative code optimization. Constructing this supervision is challenging because of heterogeneous specifications, and useful implementations emerge through iterative complicated testing and refinement. We introduce KernelMosaic, an open dataset pairing diverse CUDA tasks with verified solutions and trajectories. Human-guided review and diversity-aware selection curate tasks expressed as natural-language descriptions, reference programs, mathematical specifications, and their intersections. To build the solutions and trajectories, our agentic framework guides a strong LLM through implementation, correctness repair, and performance optimization with reusable CUDA guidance and execution feedback. Supervised fine-tuning of a small open-source model on KernelMosaic raises correctness from 4%, 0%, and 0% to 88%, 82%, and 16% on KernelBench L1, L2, and L3, respectively, while increasing the fraction of tasks with kernels faster than PyTorch eager at every level. Further training experiments show that supervision from the curated trajectories substantially outperforms direct responses and promotes sustained testing and revision. These results demonstrate that KernelMosaic enables a general-purpose model to achieve substantial gains in CUDA kernel generation.

title: An Eyring-Kramers Formula for Singular Wells

payload.title: An Eyring-Kramers Formula for Singular Wells
payload.abstract: Understanding the persistence of learned behaviors in AI safety motivates an investigation of the dynamical counterpart to the equilibrium geometry studied in singular learning theory. We analyze this persistence through transitions between singular wells. We establish an Eyring-Kramers formula for a low temperature Langevin diffusion between two compact connected zero components of a real-analytic potential. The wells may be singular and nonisolated, and the unique minimizing gate is a nondegenerate index-one saddle, with gates understood as inclusion-minimal sets meeting every minimizing path. A boundary-gate construction shows that uniqueness of this inclusion-minimal gate is equivalent to every minimizing path passing through the saddle and one such path meeting the communication level only there. Compact semianalytic topology provides a separating function away from a fixed saddle neighborhood; analytic Morse coordinates give matching capacity bounds by first sending the temperature to zero and then shrinking that neighborhood. An anchored energy estimate and a small-ball potential-theoretic identity give uniformity for deterministic starting points. The leading constant is expressed in terms of the sublevel-volume coefficient, a Gamma factor, and the saddle Hessian.

title: StructRL: Model-Free Reinforcement Learning with Replay Graphs

payload.title: StructRL: Model-Free Reinforcement Learning with Replay Graphs
payload.abstract: StructRL turns the experience collected during reinforcement learning into an explicit replay graph. Once the graph contains a path to the task goal, dynamic programming selects actions on the observed part of the state space; these actions form a graph policy that is defined only where the required transitions have been observed. StructRL transfers these actions to model-free learners: as action preferences for a DQN Q-model and as target directions along shortest observed paths for a SAC actor. For DQN on three sparse-reward MiniGrid tasks, final success rises from 0.10 to 0.90 (DoorKey), 0.10 to 0.80 (KeyCorridor) and 0 to 0.50 (ObstructedMaze); plain DQN does not catch up with three times the budget. For SAC on continuous PointMaze, graph-derived direction labels raise final success from 0.17 to 1.0 on seven matched runs that reached the goal. Distilling the graph policy into a fresh Q-model gives a DoorKey 6x6 controller that reaches the goal from 91% of reachable states, against 38% for plain DQN. Scaling experiments identify three bottlenecks: incomplete graph support, structural aliasing, and loss of graph information in high-dimensional inputs.

title: Multi-Step Underwater Acoustic Channel Prediction via Dual-Domain Structure Preservation and Pretrained Transformer

payload.title: Multi-Step Underwater Acoustic Channel Prediction via Dual-Domain Structure Preservation and Pretrained Transformer
payload.abstract: Accurate future channel state information (CSI) is essential for underwater acoustic (UWA) communication because delays associated with signal propagation, feedback, scheduling, and transceiver reconfiguration can render currently available CSI outdated. However, most existing predictors estimate only the next channel state and obtain multi-step forecasts through recursive rollout, which causes prediction errors to accumulate as the multipath structure evolves. The scarcity of sea-trial measurements further limits reliable model training. To address these challenges, we propose LLM4UACP, a dual-domain, structure-preserving framework that adapts a pretrained Transformer for few-shot multi-step UWA channel prediction. LLM4UACP extracts complementary features from the channel impulse response (CIR) and channel frequency response (CFR), aligns them through Fourier-consistent fusion, and encodes the fused representation as delay-time tokens. A pretrained Transformer with a frozen backbone is adapted through Butterfly Orthogonal Fine-tuning to jointly predict multiple future CIRs in a single forward pass, thereby avoiding the error accumulation associated with recursive prediction. Experiments on the measured SO-06 and SO-07 channels show that LLM4UACP achieves normalized mean squared error (NMSE) values of 0.0411 and 0.0399, corresponding to reductions of 88.53% and 85.15%, respectively, relative to the most recent baseline. With only 0.11M trainable parameters, LLM4UACP maintains robust performance across varying prediction horizons and observation-window lengths, limited-data settings, and cross-dataset transfer scenarios.

title: When Evaluators of AI Agents Disagree: An Empirical Study of Native Scoring, LLM Judges, and Commit-Boundary Checks on tau2-bench

payload.title: When Evaluators of AI Agents Disagree: An Empirical Study of Native Scoring, LLM Judges, and Commit-Boundary Checks on tau2-bench
payload.abstract: Agentic workflows, in which a large language model (LLM) calls tools to read and write data, are evaluated in two ways. Benchmarks compare the final state against a gold answer. Deployed services have none; an LLM judge reads the transcript and decides. Practice treats the two as interchangeable. This paper measures whether they are. We ran 2,160 episodes in tau2-bench's airline and retail domains and recorded every database write. We scored each episode four ways: native scoring against gold state, an LLM judge, that judge given the policy document, and the boundary evaluator, a minimal rule-based check of whether a write was expected against whether one occurred in the trace. Two annotators independently labeled 120 episodes for task correctness, policy compliance, and commitment correctness. The judge repeated its verdict 98.2% of the time but agreed with native scoring on 56.2%. In 11 episodes the agent executed a forbidden write. The judge passed 10 to 11, with or without the policy or transcript. A stronger judge still passed 6. The boundary evaluator, with no model call, caught all 11; no judge significantly exceeded it on human labels. Forbidden writes occurred in 11.1% of episodes without gates. Verification, correction, and safe-termination gates did not reduce them significantly. The traces show a candidate cause: the gates' evidence digest dropped the order status and customer authentication, so valid requests were rejected. The choice of evaluator decides the conclusion; the minimal check exposes failures the judges miss. Traces, code, prompts, and labels are released.

title: The norm, not the labels: training and evaluating finite-element surrogates for stress analysis in the energy norm

payload.title: The norm, not the labels: training and evaluating finite-element surrogates for stress analysis in the energy norm
payload.abstract: Finite-element surrogates predict the stresses of a new design in one evaluation, but are usually trained on solutions with a displacement loss and compared by it, although engineering decisions rest on stresses. Application in engineering: stress analysis of perforated plates and solids with cavities, parametric families in which holes concentrate stress. Contribution to artificial intelligence: training and evaluating such surrogates in the energy norm, with or without solutions, and screening their predictions without solutions. For linear elastostatics, minimising the assembled discrete potential energy is exactly supervised regression in this norm: the energy gap of a prediction is the strain energy of its stress error. A displacement loss under-weights the stiff modes that carry the strains. In pre-registered comparisons, changing only the norm of the supervised loss cut a three-dimensional transformer's median energy-norm error 7.5-fold and its median von Mises error 6.1-fold; in two dimensions it more than halved the von Mises error, also on held-out instances. In three dimensions, the transformer trained on the energy alone came within a factor of 1.3 of the energy-norm-supervised one in median energy-norm and von Mises error. It was more accurate than the displacement-supervised one on all five metrics in every seed. Given the stiffness matrix, a Ritz projection was more accurate than the label-free transformer, in the seed means, on every metric but peak stress. No network transferred to a substantially finer mesh. The energy ranks predictions of a load case, and its sign flags those worse than the zero field.

title: Beyond the First Hit: Towards Tight Guarantees for $k$-means++

payload.title: Beyond the First Hit: Towards Tight Guarantees for $k$-means++
payload.abstract: Let $R_k$ be the worst-case ratio between the expected cost of the $k$ seeds chosen by $k$-means++ and the optimal $k$-means cost. In their seminal paper introducing $k$-means++, Arthur and Vassilvitskii (SODA 2007) showed that $2\ln k\le R_k\le8(\ln k+2)$, and Makarychev, Reddy and Shan (NeurIPS 2020) improved the upper bound to $5(\ln k+2)$. We prove $R_k\le\frac{1163}{233}+2.108\,H_{k-2}$ for every $k\ge3$ by a computer-assisted argument, and $R_k\le5+2.3139\,H_{k-2}$ for every $k\ge2$ by a short analytic argument; here $H_j$ is the $j$th harmonic number. Since $H_{k-2}\le1+\ln k$, this lowers the leading coefficient of $\ln k$ from $5$ to $2.108$. We also determine $R_2=5$ and $R_3=185/32$ exactly; both are suprema that are approached but not attained. On the lower side we prove $R_k\ge2(1+H_{k-1})$ for every $k$, and give a second family of lower bounds that is larger than this for $2\le k\le18$. Previous analyses bound the expected cost of a cluster just after it is first sampled by a constant times its optimal cost, and then charge that cost for the rest of the run. We instead track how a cluster's cost evolves after its first hit: a cluster left with a large residual cost is likely to be sampled again before it accumulates much of the logarithmic charge, and each repeat repairs it.

title: MechFoundry: An agentic loop that poses and performs engineering analyses and optimization of real-world objects

payload.title: MechFoundry: An agentic loop that poses and performs engineering analyses and optimization of real-world objects
payload.abstract: AI agents can automate software engineering because a compiler or a test suite checks that the code does what the user or the agent intended. In engineering analysis, however, the steps that precede the computation have few easily verifiable checks: modeling a design or an object, deciding how it is used, where supports and loads are applied, and what material each part is made of. A human expert therefore makes these decisions, carries out the steps, and judges the result, one object at a time. We present MechFoundry, an agentic loop coupled with bespoke software that automates structural analyses of real-world objects without a human in the loop. From an object's lexical description, it generates a shape, poses a loading case relevant to how the object is used, assigns a material to each part, solves the nonlinear structural response, and improves the design against the loads it carries. A differentiable GPU solver built on an adaptive octree that need not conform to the surface enables the transition from shape generation to simulation and optimization. Across 50 everyday and engineering objects, the agent posed and solved a loading case in 6.5 minutes and for US$1.3 per object on average. Without a test suite to check against, we had language-model reviewers grade each session, as a first indication of where the agent's engineering judgment holds and where it fails.

title: Deep learning-guided discovery reveals the diversity and mutational potential of environmental beta-lactamases

payload.title: Deep learning-guided discovery reveals the diversity and mutational potential of environmental beta-lactamases
payload.abstract: Beta-lactamases are a major mechanism of bacterial resistance to beta-lactam antibiotics; however, their functional diversity and mutational potential in environmental microbial communities remain partially understood. This study aimed to characterize environmental beta-lactamase diversity and investigate how sequence variation influences antibiotic resistance. By integrating protein language model (PLMs) with ensemble learning, we identified more than 46,000 putative beta-lactamases across all four Ambler classes from environmental metagenomes, widely distributed across diverse habitats, with distinct habitat-associated class compositions. The candidates sharing approximately 30% sequence identity with known beta-lactamases conferred resistance to multiple beta-lactam antibiotics when expressed in Escherichia coli. Combining inverse folding model with PLMs further identified mutations that altered resistance profiles, including substitutions that increased resistance to carbapenems. Predicted high-fitness sites exhibited greater natural sequence variability overall, with higher variability in wastewater-derived than ocean-derived enzymes. These findings reveal undercharacterized beta-lactamase diversity and substantial mutational flexibility in environmental microbiomes, providing a basis for investigating their potential contribution to the diversification of antibiotic resistance.

title: Provenance-tracked, experimentally validated neural operator surrogates of three-dimensional laser melting with keyholes and free-form paths

payload.title: Provenance-tracked, experimentally validated neural operator surrogates of three-dimensional laser melting with keyholes and free-form paths
payload.abstract: A three-dimensional thermo-fluid-dynamic simulation of laser melting resolves the melt pool and vapor depression but costs from one to thousands of core-hours per track. We train FNO, RIGNO and GAOT neural operators that predict the temperature, melt-pool and free-surface fields. Our datasets comprise 3D temperature and melt geometry fields covering lack-of-fusion to keyhole conditions under varied laser power, scan speed, beam radius, beam shape and preheat, and include free-form scan paths with speed changes and up to four beams. We generate them with FLOW-3D WELD, using solver settings validated against published measurements for four materials. We implement an AiiDA framework to store the provenance of every simulation, model and evaluation, so each tabulated metric traces back to the solver and model inputs behind it. On held-out simulations, the best architecture scores below 2 % relative temperature error on quasi-steady straight tracks, below 4 % on single-beam free-form paths and about 5 % with two to four beams. Inference takes under a second per predicted arbitrary time step on our single-GPU setup. We extend a surrogate trained on Ti-6Al-4V to Inconel 718 by growing its training set autonomously, and the extended models reach a relative temperature error of about 3 % or less on both Inconel 718 and Ti-6Al-4V. At 20 Ti-6Al-4V and Inconel 718 conditions held out of training, the two-alloy RIGNO predicts melt-pool and vapor-depression depths within 30 % of published measurements, and its depths differ from FLOW-3D at the same conditions by 2 % on average. Furthermore, these results provide a scalable framework which can readily be applied to computationally intensive simulations in fields other than laser melting.

title: AVA: Agentic Variant Adjudication for Automated, Auditable Read-Level Review in Cancer Diagnostic Sequencing

payload.title: AVA: Agentic Variant Adjudication for Automated, Auditable Read-Level Review in Cancer Diagnostic Sequencing
payload.abstract: Identifying a tumor's DNA mutations is central to cancer diagnosis and treatment, but distinguishing genuine mutations from sequencing artifacts is error-prone. In practice, genuine mutations are identified using fixed variant-allele-frequency (VAF) and depth thresholds which cannot separate artifacts from genuine mutations in the borderline low-VAF zone where they overlap. A laboratory specialist must manually inspect the read-level sequencing data, a slow step that has high inter-rater variability and causes diagnosis delays. We present AVA: Agentic Variant Adjudication; an agentic framework that automates this read-level inspection with subagents that reason over evidence, generate investigative code, and return a real-or-artifact adjudications with an auditable reasoning trace all without training on existing data. On both the SEQC2 DNA-seq benchmark and patient RNA-seq data, restricted to a subsample of borderline variants where thresholds fail, both closed-source (Claude Sonnet 5) and open-weight (GLM 5.3 Flash and Gemma 4 31b) agents outperform the best achievable VAF/depth thresholds. Ultimately, AVA is suited for privacy-constrained clinical deployment, since the framework can run on locally deployed open-weight models with descriptive reasoning traces to keep specialists in the loop.

title: Selecting Person Segmentation Models for Real-Time Video Call Backgrounds on the CPU

payload.title: Selecting Person Segmentation Models for Real-Time Video Call Backgrounds on the CPU
payload.abstract: Background blur and background replacement are now normal parts of a video call. Many open models and open source pipelines can do this, but it is hard to know which one to pick. Speed, edge quality and license all matter, and they are often reported on different hardware, or not reported at all. In this work we ran 20 setups on the same laptop CPU, with the same 640x480 frames and the same output view. The setups are 15 open models and 5 complete open source pipelines. We measured frames per second on a test clip and on a live webcam, compared the masks on a public domain portrait and on three video call photos with a raised hand, one of them a close front camera view, and recorded the license of every model. The fastest setups reach more than 40 frames per second on a laptop CPU, while the slowest, a high detail model for still images, needs several seconds per frame. A few setups give clean edges and still run in real time. We also found that the runtime library and the steps around the model can change the speed by several times. Based on these results we give a guide that tells the reader which model to choose for a given need, such as a weak laptop, the best hair edges, a closed source product, or people behind the speaker.

title: Probe Before You Preach: Conformal Ambiguity Sets and Neuro-Symbolic Counterfactual Probing for Diagnosing Algebraic Misconceptions in Middle School Mathematics

payload.title: Probe Before You Preach: Conformal Ambiguity Sets and Neuro-Symbolic Counterfactual Probing for Diagnosing Algebraic Misconceptions in Middle School Mathematics
payload.abstract: Distinct mathematical misconception rules can produce the same incorrect answer, making diagnosis from a single response ambiguous. We formalize this algebraic collision and derive a conditional Bayes error bound; internally generated reasoning does not add student-specific information beyond its inputs under an explicit conditional-independence assumption. We propose Mondrian Adaptive Conformal Misconception Sets (MACMS) and Symbolic-Verified Counterfactual Micro-Probing (Sym-EIG). MACMS has curriculum-group marginal coverage under exchangeability, not a per-student correctness guarantee. Sym-EIG searches for probes whose outputs separate modeled candidate rules; identification additionally depends on the candidate set and response model. An audit of a local public Eedi graph finds 2,118 of 2,258 linked constructs associated with at least two misconception IDs; construct-level associations alone do not establish same-answer collisions. Other project performance tables require recomputation because their script assigns numerical results directly. No diagnostic performance or classroom learning benefit is claimed here. A classroom study is proposed for future validation.

title: SideTaskBench: Measuring Unauthorized Side-Task Delivery in Coding Agents

payload.title: SideTaskBench: Measuring Unauthorized Side-Task Delivery in Coding Agents
payload.abstract: Can a coding agent fix a user's repository while also completing and delivering work the user never requested? In this paper, we introduce SideTaskBench to measure this failure where third-party technical references induce agents to produce independent side-task artifacts during an authorized repair. Repair success alone misses this behavior. Our key measurement contribution is to pair each repair with a self-contained side task and verify side tasks' delivery success rate along with the repair success rate. The benchmark contains 25 Python repairs and 190 side-task units. Its four-level similarity index defines 300 executable repair--side-task pairs. The experiments show roughly 40% valid delivery under wrapped requests for two models, alongside repair success close to their clean baselines. The completed v10 similarity run uses DeepSeek-V4-Flash on all 300 pairs, with eight repetitions per pair (2,400 runs). Conditional delivery ranges from 20.48% for L0 unrelated tasks to 57.44% for L3 mechanism-overlapping tasks, while the L1-L0 difference is 5.37 percentage points and remains sensitive to task composition. The central insight is that technical relevance may blur the authorization boundary for an agent, such that an agent can solve the requested problem and still deliver unauthorized work. SideTaskBench emphasizes this potential weakness of existing agents and provides a testbed for defenses that preserve repair capability while preventing unauthorized delivery. The code is available at: https://github.com/xywen97/SideTaskBench.

title: metalSPARSE: A 2:4 Semi-Structured Sparse GEMV Kernel for Apple Silicon GPUs

payload.title: metalSPARSE: A 2:4 Semi-Structured Sparse GEMV Kernel for Apple Silicon GPUs
payload.abstract: Autoregressive Large Language Models (LLMs) generate text one token at a time, and each token reads every weight from memory, so on edge devices, decoding is limited by memory bandwidth. 2:4 semi-structured sparsity keeps two of every four weights, but Apple-silicon GPUs have no sparse matrix hardware, so pruning helps only if a kernel actually reads fewer bytes. We present metalSPARSE, to our knowledge the first 2:4 sparse kernels for Apple GPUs, together with a fused decoder written in Metal. The kernels stream weights in compressed form and expand them in registers. On Qwen2.5-1.5B with 2:4 sparsity on every decoder linear layer, decoding runs 3.6x faster than HuggingFace Transformers on PyTorch-MPS on an 8 GB M2 MacBook Air and 1.52x faster than MLX on a 16 GB M4. The same engine on dense weights matches MLX, so the gain comes from the compressed weights, and sparsity delivers 97% of the speedup its byte reduction allows. Prompt processing, which is compute-bound, does not speed up. To preserve quality, we combine a Wanda mask with block-wise reconstruction and low-rank adapters trained jointly with the surviving weights and quantized to 4 bits. On WikiText-2 this brings perplexity from 3.01x dense after one-shot pruning (Wanda with a closed-form refit) to 1.34x, and the whole pipeline runs on the same laptop/hardware.

title: Zugwise: Domain-Aware Game Reconstruction for Digitizing Handwritten Chess Scoresheets

payload.title: Zugwise: Domain-Aware Game Reconstruction for Digitizing Handwritten Chess Scoresheets
payload.abstract: Digitizing handwritten chess scoresheets has been studied as a handwriting-recognition problem: read the move in each box and check that it is legal. This framing misses the errors that matter most. A misread that yields an illegal move is loud. One that yields a legal-but-wrong move is silent, because a legality-only pipeline accepts it and reads every later move against a wrong position. We therefore treat the task as game reconstruction and present Zugwise, which repurposes computer-chess machinery (quiescence search, static exchange evaluation, pin detection) to ask not "what should be played?" but "could a human plausibly have written this?" An absurdity detector makes silent errors loud at or near where they occur, and a backward search traces late symptoms to their cause. Candidate ranking excludes chess-quality signals. A Needleman-Wunsch merge adds the second player's sheet as evidence, and review stops send every disagreement between the sheets' legal readings to a human. In oracle replay of two tournament sections, a release adding them cuts silent errors from 16 to 1 and from 50 to 13. Two learned signals, CTC re-scoring against the recognizer's raw output and a Maia-style human-move prior, raise the correct fix's top-rank rate from 58.8% to 78.0% of the replacement decisions where it is a candidate, and hold without refitting on a later section. On the first section, the human-verified output matches an independent expert transcription move for move on 34 of 45 games, and adjudication against the sheets found errors in both records, on different plies. We do not establish that either workflow is faster or more accurate. The system runs entirely in the browser and is free, private, and offline-capable; alongside it we offer a three-way adjudication protocol for a domain where no single record is ground truth.

title: Modelling the occurrence and reporting dynamics of weather-related home insurance claims

payload.title: Modelling the occurrence and reporting dynamics of weather-related home insurance claims
payload.abstract: We study the occurrence and reporting dynamics of weather-related claims in private home insurance, combining detailed portfolio and claim information with publicly available high-resolution weather data. Existing approaches typically start from an identified severe weather event, such as a hailstorm, and model the dynamics of the claims caused by that event. In practice, however, claims arise under moderate as well as severe conditions, and the claims handling process runs continuously. An insurer therefore requires insight into the occurrence and reporting of claims on every calendar day. Modelling all calendar days jointly poses two challenges: recently occurred claims are only partially reported, and days with severe weather are rare while accounting for a large share of the claims. We propose a multi-regime EM-XGBoost framework that addresses both: an expectation-maximisation setup accounts for the incurred-but-not-reported (IBNR) claims, while a data-driven regime structure lets the occurrence and reporting dynamics differ across weather conditions. In a case study on a Dutch home insurance portfolio, we compare single- and two-regime specifications for two spatial resolutions: the country as a whole, and its individual regions. We find that the regional two-regime model outperforms the regional single-regime model as well as both national models, indicating that the benefit of a multi-regime setting depends on a sufficiently granular spatial resolution. We also show that daily covariates constructed from hourly weather observations, capturing the duration and the intra-day timing of severe weather, improve both the occurrence and the reporting model.

title: Katz Kernel Based Stratification of Breast Cancer Patients

payload.title: Katz Kernel Based Stratification of Breast Cancer Patients
payload.abstract: The integration of mechanistic signaling networks into clinical research has become a cornerstone of precision oncology. By capturing the complex biochemical interactions within a cell, these networks provide a functional map of disease progression that goes beyond simple genomic mutations. Consequently, the development of specific signaling models of patients has significant relevance, allowing for a more granular representation of individual disease profiles. In this setting, there is a growing need for robust methodologies capable of comparing graph based pathway structures to identify similarities and differences across patient cohorts. Such comparisons are essential for the identification of clinically meaningful subgroups, and the discovery of novel biomarkers. Standard graph kernels, while mathematically rigorous, often remain too generic for this purpose. They frequently fail to capture features specific to gene signaling networks, resulting in suboptimal clustering performance. In this paper, we present a domain specific graph kernel designed for mechanistic signaling networks. Unlike generic approaches, our method explicitly incorporates biological constraints and gene interaction patterns into the kernel formulation, enabling a more accurate characterization of both topological structure and functional behavior. We assess its performance on breast cancer datasets, focusing on its ability to support disease subtyping. Our results suggest that our approach can effectively contribute to patient stratification.

title: Kernel Adaptive Deformable Convolution for Remote Sensing Object Detection.

payload.title: Kernel Adaptive Deformable Convolution for Remote Sensing Object Detection.
payload.abstract: Modeling geometric variations, particularly the extreme fluctuations in scale and shape, stands as a persistent challenge in computer vision, which is significantly exacerbated in remote sensing object detection (RSOD). Existing methods are often constrained by the fixed geometric topology of standard convolutions or the insufficient representation power of linear feature aggregation, making it difficult to strike an ideal balance between adaptability and computational efficiency. To address these challenges, we propose a novel scale- and shape-adaptive method named Kernel Adaptive Deformable Convolution (KAD-Conv). Specifically, KAD-Conv employs a specialized Deformable Spatial Convolution (DSC) at its core to adaptively adjust sampling locations, while reformulating the mask generation process to fully leverage the mask's potential for discriminative feature modulation. In KAD-Conv, we further introduce a Scale-aware Kernel Adaptive mechanism, which enables the dynamic adjustment of sampling scales to effectively capture object representations across extreme scale variations without increasing kernel size. With KAD-Conv, we develop a novel object detection network based on Multi-task Guided Learning (MGL), called KAD-CNet. Extensive experiments conducted on widely used remote sensing benchmark datasets, including DOTA-v1.0, DIOR, and NWPU VHR-10, along with validation on natural scenes exhibiting extreme geometric variations, have validated the effectiveness of the proposed KAD-CNet. Moreover, comprehensive comparisons against various YOLO-series models further underscore the practical value and efficiency of the proposed approach.
payload.journal: IEEE Trans Pattern Anal Mach Intell

title: Person Recognition at Altitude and Range: Fusion of Face, Body Shape and Gait.

payload.title: Person Recognition at Altitude and Range: Fusion of Face, Body Shape and Gait.
payload.abstract: We address the problem of whole-body person recognition in unconstrained environments.
